cases.abstract: Prediction sets can be calibrated for graded errors, not only for whether they contain the correct label. Conformal risk control chooses a parameter from calibration losses after adding a finite-sample correction that accounts for an unseen observation. For exchangeable, bounded, right-continuous losses that decrease with the parameter and admit a sufficiently safe endpoint, this choice keeps expected test loss at or below a user-specified target. With independent, identically distributed nonnegative losses and zero probability of a jump at any prespecified parameter, the achieved expectation is also at least the target minus 2B/(n + 1), where B bounds the loss; examples establish the sharpness of this general lower bound. Applications to segmentation, multilabel and hierarchical classification, and question answering illustrate control of nonbinary losses over 1,000 random data splits. The guarantee concerns expectation over calibration and test data, rather than a bound for every fitted prediction set. Monotonicity is consequential: without it, expected loss can approach B despite a lower requested target. A monotone upper envelope restores control but can sacrifice informativeness when the original loss is far from monotone.
cases.methods: Calibration replaces the unknown test risk with the average of n observed loss functions, but does not threshold that average alone. It selects the smallest parameter satisfying [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n + 1) <= alpha, using the maximum parameter if no value qualifies, provided that endpoint itself has loss at most alpha. The additional B term treats the unseen loss at its worst allowed value. To justify this operation, the proof compares the selected parameter with an oracle computed from all n + 1 losses. Exchangeability makes the test loss uniformly distributed among these losses conditional on their multiset; right-continuity allows the oracle to meet its threshold. Monotonicity then ensures that the implementable choice cannot have greater loss than the oracle. This converts an empirical calibration rule into finite-sample expected-risk control without requiring the underlying predictor to supply calibrated probabilities.
cases.results: At a target false-negative rate of 0.1, polyp segmentation produced a mean risk of 0.0987 with standard deviation 0.0114 across 1,000 random splits, using 1,000 calibration images and 781 evaluation images per split. Multilabel classification on MS COCO, with 4,000 calibration and 1,000 evaluation images, yielded 0.0996 with standard deviation 0.0052 under the same target and split count. Both means are close to the requested level, while the segmentation results show greater variation across splits; these different tasks and calibration sizes do not isolate the source of that difference. The interpretation is risk calibration rather than universal success: a mean near 0.1 does not require every split or image to satisfy that threshold. The theoretical counterexample supplies the complementary boundary. For nonmonotone losses, the same unmodified rule can produce expected loss arbitrarily near its upper bound B, so the positive application results cannot justify dispensing with monotonicity.
cases.notes: The application statistics describe variation across random splits, not confidence intervals or independent training runs. The tight lower bound needs stronger assumptions than the upper guarantee. The multilabel prose says false positives although the defined loss is a false-negative fraction; the question-answering threshold direction and the shift section's monotonicity wording also merit checking against the theorem.

cases.abstract: Nonstationary data can make a fixed conformal calibration level yield the wrong coverage even when prediction models and score quantiles are repeatedly refitted. Adaptive conformal inference adjusts that level online using the latest observed coverage error: a miss shifts calibration toward larger sets, whereas a covered response shifts it toward smaller ones. The feedback recursion yields a distribution-free guarantee that the long-run empirical miscoverage frequency converges to the chosen target, with a finite-horizon discrepancy bound. This guarantee does not establish target coverage at each time point. Stronger concentration and approximate marginal-coverage results are derived in a hidden Markov setting with fixed score and quantile functions and stationary initialization, with additional regularity conditions. Stock-volatility forecasting and time-zone-ordered county vote prediction illustrate how adaptation can reduce local coverage departures relative to a fixed level. However, volatility experiments with unnormalized scores exhibit substantially wider coverage swings, showing that feedback does not eliminate dependence on score design. The step size balances responsiveness against instability, and the procedure requires each response to be observed before the next update.
cases.methods: Let alpha be the desired miscoverage frequency and alpha_t the level supplied to the score quantile at time t. After observing whether the prediction set misses the response, the algorithm updates alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha - err_t), where err_t is one for a miss and gamma is positive. Lowering alpha_t raises the quantile threshold, counteracting undercoverage; increasing it reverses that adjustment. The distribution-free analysis sums this recursion, expressing cumulative miscoverage error through the difference between the initial and final levels. Quantile conventions outside [0, 1] produce full or empty sets, keeping the levels bounded and making the average discrepancy vanish as the horizon grows. This operation controls accumulated coverage error without modelling the shift, but permits extreme sets and does not by itself guarantee accurate coverage in short windows.
cases.results: With normalized volatility errors, adaptive calibration at a 90% coverage target kept the reported 500-day local coverage curves within the variation illustrated by an independent Bernoulli comparator. Fixed-level calibration showed larger departures, including undercoverage for Fannie Mae during the 2008 crisis. The four displayed stocks were selected from twelve because the fixed method failed visibly, so those panels emphasize failure cases rather than a representative sample. Both methods used GARCH forecasts and score quantiles based on rolling 1,250-day histories; changing to unnormalized absolute errors made the adaptive curves fluctuate much more widely. That contrast supports score stabilization as a consequential part of adaptation, rather than attributing satisfactory coverage to feedback alone. In the county-vote experiment, counties were ordered by time zone and randomized within zones. Adaptive calibration maintained approximately 90% local coverage while the fixed method developed troughs around zone changes. These observations concern local coverage under the tested constructions, not guaranteed coverage at every time or evidence of shorter intervals.
cases.notes: Reported local coverage is descriptive; the Bernoulli curves are visual comparators, not significance tests. The county ordering approximates east-to-west reporting drift rather than replaying the actual election-night sequence. The stronger hidden Markov results assume fixed fitted functions and stationary initialization, unlike the rolling refitting used in the examples. The stock coverage formula uses centered 500-day windows despite surrounding prose describing recent history; the draft avoids identifying the windows as trailing.
